misconceptions.description: The learner treats the limit as another name for evaluation, so a missing or displaced function value is read as a missing or displaced limit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give a graph with an open circle at one height and a closed point at another over the same input and ask for the limit and the value separately.
misconceptions.name: The limit at a point is the value of the function there

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a single one sided approach as sufficient, so a jump is read as a limit equal to the value on whichever side was examined.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the left hand limit and the right hand limit as separate answers, then ask whether the two sided limit exists.
misconceptions.name: A limit exists whenever the function approaches something on one side

misconceptions.description: The learner expects the function to attain the limit value, so a function that approaches without attaining is read as having no limit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether a function can have a limit at an input where it is undefined, and ask for an example.
misconceptions.name: A limit is a prediction the function must eventually reach

misconceptions.description: The learner treats tabulated agreement as proof, so oscillation or behaviour between the tabulated inputs is not considered.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what the function does at inputs between two adjacent rows of the table.
misconceptions.name: A table settles the behaviour of a function

misconceptions.description: The learner applies the quotient and composite theorems as formal rules without the denominator condition or the continuity condition on the outer function.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to state the condition each theorem requires and to point to where it was checked.
misconceptions.name: Limit theorems apply unconditionally

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the symbol zero over zero as an answer, reading it as zero, as undefined, or as a nonexistence verdict rather than as a signal to rewrite.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give two expressions with the same indeterminate form and different limits and ask for both values.
misconceptions.name: An indeterminate form is a value

misconceptions.description: The learner treats cancellation as a syntactic move on repeated symbols rather than a division of common factors, so terms are cancelled like factors.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to evaluate the original and the rewritten expression at one convenient input and compare.
misconceptions.name: Rewriting an expression may change any matching symbols

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the bounding functions as things to evaluate at the target rather than as functions whose limits must agree, and handles the inequality as an equation.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the bounding inequality must hold at the target input itself for the theorem to apply.
misconceptions.name: The squeeze theorem is a substitution rule

misconceptions.description: The learner holds one of the three conditions as the whole definition, most often that the function is defined there or that the one sided limits agree.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Give one function defined at the point with unequal one sided limits and one whose limit exists but differs from the value, and ask about continuity in both.
misconceptions.name: Continuity is a single condition

misconceptions.description: The learner treats naming the definition or the theorem as the argument, so the values and conditions that make the claim true are never produced.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask which feature of the given function or table makes the stated claim true.
misconceptions.name: Restating a definition counts as a justification

misconceptions.description: The learner reads any zero of the original denominator as unbounded behaviour without simplifying first.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the limit of the expression at that input after factoring numerator and denominator.
misconceptions.name: Every input missing from the domain is an asymptote

misconceptions.description: The learner treats an infinite limit as a two sided property and writes one statement where the two sides carry opposite signs, or reads the infinity symbol as a real value.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the sign of the quotient just to the left and just to the right of the input.
misconceptions.name: Unbounded behaviour is the same on both sides

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the infinity symbol as an input value, so end behaviour is computed by substitution and the conditions on degree comparison are skipped.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to divide numerator and denominator by the dominant power and to say what each resulting term approaches.
misconceptions.name: Infinity is a number that can be substituted

misconceptions.description: The learner treats a statement about the long run rate as a statement about the long run amount, so the wrong function is placed inside the limit.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the units of the limit just written and compare them with the units the question asks about.
misconceptions.name: The end behaviour of a quantity and of its rate are interchangeable

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the stated setting as discharging the hypotheses of a theorem, so continuity is asserted rather than derived from a stated property.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask what in the question establishes that the function is continuous on the interval.
misconceptions.name: A hypothesis is satisfied because the question implies it

misconceptions.description: The learner reads the conclusion of the Intermediate Value Theorem as producing a unique input, or applies it without checking that the target lies between the endpoint values.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask whether the theorem rules out a second input with the same output and what it would take to find one.
misconceptions.name: An existence theorem locates or counts solutions

misconceptions.description: The learner treats the difference quotient over an interval as the rate at an instant, so no limiting process is invoked.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the average rate over two different intervals containing the same point and ask which one is the rate at that point.
misconceptions.name: An average rate over an interval is the rate at a point in it

misconceptions.description: The learner does not separate a limit whose value is infinite from a limit taken as the variable grows without bound, so vertical and horizontal asymptote statements are exchanged.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask the student to point to where the infinity symbol sits in each of two statements and to say what each claims.
misconceptions.name: All limit notation with an infinity symbol means the same thing

misconceptions.description: The learner reports a function as continuous everywhere because its formula belongs to a family continuous on its domain, without excluding the inputs outside that domain.
misconceptions.discriminating_probe: Ask for the inputs at which the expression is undefined before any interval is written.
misconceptions.name: Continuity is a property of a formula rather than of a domain
